about.title: Stories people *finish.*
paragraphs: I'm Praise Ucho, a writer who turns products, ideas, and complex topics into stories that hold attention and move people to act.

My work runs on one belief: strategy decides what a brand says, and story decides whether anyone listens. I take time to understand the product, the brand, and the people it's meant to reach before I write a word, then refine until the work fits the vision and does its job.
Four years of writing stand behind that claim, two of them scripting stories; the craft has been daily practice long before it became a career.

works.title: Why Customers Buy Stories, Not Just Products
works.proves: narrative structure that makes a marketing idea feel human.
works.body:
People don't just buy products. They buy the story they believe the product will help them live.

Imagine you're scrolling through Instagram. The first post says: 50% OFF! LIMITED STOCK! BUY NOW! You scroll past without thinking.

Then another post catches your attention. It's a short video of a young woman getting ready for her first job interview. Before she leaves the house, she reaches for a perfume sitting on her dressing table, a gift from her mother on graduation day. She sprays it on, smiles at herself in the mirror, takes a deep breath, and walks out the door.

> “Confidence isn't always loud. Sometimes, it smells familiar.”

Without realizing it, you've watched the entire video. You didn't stop because of the perfume. You stopped because of the story.

That's the difference between selling a product and selling a feeling. A story.

Consumers are exposed to an estimated 4,000 to 10,000 advertisements every day. Most are forgotten almost immediately, because they all compete the same way: shouting for attention and pushing for an immediate transaction. “Buy now.” “Limited offer.” “20% off, ending today.” Eventually, every ad starts sounding generic.

Yet every once in a while, one stays with us — not because it was louder or cheaper, but because it made us feel something. That's the power of storytelling.

Businesses often believe customers buy because of features and specifications. Those things matter, but if features alone sold products, every company offering similar quality at a similar price would enjoy the same success. They don't — because people mostly buy on emotion, and justify the decision with logic afterward.

# Excerpt from a 1,540-word article. The full version is available on request.

works.title: Fiction Excerpt
works.proves: an original voice with full command of tension and rhythm.
works.body:
The storytelling instinct that guides the samples above also drives my fiction. A brief piece in a different tone:

I hear it, my name.

I look around, hoping it's someone else, but no.

He points at me…gesturing for me to wait.

My heart drops to my stomach. Not fear…just that sinking disappointment.

He starts walking towards me. Slowly.

Everything else fades. The noise. The movement. The people.

It's just that one sound now, my name being called, and it's what put me to a halt. I freeze.

… I hate it.

Being called. Being noticed. Being put in the spotlight. It does something to me.

Something I can't explain…

This time,

> …it's already too late to run.
